claims.reason: Backed by quotes only (no dependency row). claims.reason: Weakest part: 'żądania alternatywy'. Backed: refusal matters where processing rests on consent, and consent counts as voluntary only if the person can refuse without adverse consequences (recital 42; UODO school case); Art. 9(2) has other conditions that need no consent, so the possibility of refusing depends on which basis applies. Not backed: no snapshot says a person may demand an alternative method in any context; the UODO lecture only asks the controller whether a choice can be offered (line 94).

claims.claim: Ta porada dotyczy organizacji przetwarzającej biometrię, nie jest oceną lokalnego odblokowania urządzenia.
Tekst opisuje przepisy ogólnie, nie jest poradą prawną i nie miał przeglądu prawnika.

scope_gaps.note: Title tells the person to ask about an alternative; the sources frame alternatives as the controller's own assessment, not as something the person can ask for or obtain.

Art. 13 applies when data are collected from the person and lapses where the person already has the information (Art. 13(4)); the sentence says 'organizacja' in general, while the snapshots cover only GDPR duties of controllers, not other regimes.
Sources speak to controllers (assess alternatives, consider a choice); the sentence addresses the individual.

Art. 4(14) also requires that the data relate to physical, physiological or behavioural characteristics of a person; the sentence names only the technical-processing and identification elements and does not claim to be the whole definition.
Art. 9(4) lets Member States keep or add further conditions or limits for biometric data; not mentioned in the sentence and not claimed.

Reader might assume that an Art. 9(2) condition alone makes processing lawful. The UODO lecture (lines 71-72) says one condition suffices; recital 51 (lines 656-658) says the general rules, including the conditions of lawfulness, still apply. The sentence says neither.

The second cited snapshot is a UODO online lecture (28 April 2021), a regulator's interpretation, not a legal norm; the sentence does not call it one, but a reader might assume the norm label covers it.

The support is recital 51, a preamble that explains the operative text, not an operative article. The recital says photographs should not always be special-category data; the sentence says 'zdjęcie' and 'automatycznie', consistent with that.

No snapshot addresses a right to demand an alternative method; the dependence of refusal on context and legal basis is shown only through consent (recital 42, UODO school case) versus the other Art. 9(2) conditions.
